step: Obtain apostilled/legalised non-criminal record certificate for Work Permit Notification application
authority: Home-country police or justice authority; Chinese Embassy for legalisation
deadline_label: Start 8–10 weeks before target departure; must be complete before employer's MOHRSS application
non_obvious_official_guidance: MOHRSS work permit applications require a non-criminal record certificate from the applicant's country of origin or most recent country of residence, authenticated through the Chinese embassy or consulate.
non_obvious_actual_reality: China is not a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, so an apostille alone is insufficient. Documents must follow a three-step chain: (1) local notarisation, (2) home-country foreign ministry authentication, (3) Chinese embassy legalisation. Some countries now issue e-apostilles — Chinese authorities may not accept these; verify with the specific Chinese embassy before proceeding. The full chain can take 6–10 weeks.
non_obvious_action_required: Initiate the certificate and legalisation chain immediately on assignment confirmation. Confirm the Chinese embassy in the applicant's country has not recently changed its legalisation requirements. Keep original plus at least two certified copies.
source: MOHRSS Foreign Workers Work Permit Service Platform — Application Requirements

step: Chinese employer applies for Work Permit Notification via MOHRSS online platform
authority: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS)
form_name: 外国人来华工作许可申请表 (Foreigner Work Permit Application Form)
field_label: Work Permit Notification Letter (来华工作许可通知)
deadline_label: Complete at least 4–8 weeks before Z visa appointment; must precede Z visa application
non_obvious_official_guidance: The employing entity applies through the Foreign Workers Work Permit Service Platform. Workers are classified Category A (high-end talent), Category B (professional), or Category C (general labour); Category B requires a points-based eligibility score.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Processing times vary significantly by city: Beijing and Shanghai average 2–3 weeks; smaller cities may take 4–6 weeks. The employer entity must be registered on the MOHRSS platform before applying (registration takes 3–5 business days). Category C workers require special justification and approval is not automatic. The notification letter is valid for 60 days only.
non_obvious_action_required: Register the employing entity on the MOHRSS platform well before the assignment start. Confirm the employee's category classification. Collect: employee degree certificate, CV, passport copy, legalised non-criminal record certificate, signed employment contract, and company business licence. Monitor the online system status — incomplete documents restart the processing clock.
source: MOHRSS Foreign Workers Work Permit Service Platform

step: Obtain Foreigner Physical Examination Certificate from a designated health facility
authority: International Travel Healthcare Centre (designated facility in applicant's country or in China)
form_name: 外国人体格检查记录 (Foreigner Physical Examination Record)
deadline_label: Before Z visa application; certificate valid for 6 months from examination date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Applicants for Z (work) visas are required to present a physical examination certificate completed at a facility recognised by the Chinese authorities covering specified communicable disease and general health parameters.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Requirements vary by Chinese embassy: some require the examination at a designated hospital in the applicant's home country; others accept completion after arrival at a Chinese International Travel Healthcare Centre. The exam screens for tuberculosis, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and mental health conditions. A positive HIV result can lead to Z visa refusal. Required examination forms and designated facility lists are not always prominently published on embassy websites.
non_obvious_action_required: Check the specific Chinese embassy or consulate website for the list of designated examination facilities and the exact form version required. Book early — some designated facilities have 2–3 week wait times. Bring the original certificate (not a copy) to the visa appointment.
source: National Immigration Administration — Entry Visa Health Requirements

step: Apply for Z (work) visa at Chinese Embassy or Consulate General in home country
authority: Chinese Embassy or Consulate General in applicant's country
form_name: 签证申请表 (Visa Application Form V.2013)
deadline_label: After receipt of Work Permit Notification; allow 5–10 business days processing at embassy
non_obvious_official_guidance: The Z visa is the sole visa category permitting employment in mainland China. Applicants must present the original Work Permit Notification issued by MOHRSS.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Z visa is typically single-entry with a 30-day stay duration — it is not a long-term authorisation. The employee must convert it to a Residence Permit within 30 days of arrival; failure renders the stay unlawful and attracts fines of CNY 500 per day. The Z visa has no fixed start date but must be activated before the Work Permit Notification expires (60-day validity). Z visas must generally be applied for at a Chinese embassy, not a commercial visa application centre.
non_obvious_action_required: Required documents typically include: original Work Permit Notification, physical examination certificate, signed employment contract, valid passport (minimum 6 months beyond intended stay), completed visa application form, and passport-size photos. Confirm exact requirements with the specific Chinese embassy — documents required vary by applicant nationality and mission. Apply early enough that the Notification does not expire before the visa is issued.

step: Register temporary residence at local police substation (派出所) within 24 hours of arrival at non-hotel accommodation
authority: Public Security Bureau (PSB) — local police substation (派出所)
form_name: 临时住宿登记表 (Temporary Accommodation Registration Form)
deadline_label: Within 24 hours of arriving at non-hotel private accommodation; hotels report automatically
non_obvious_official_guidance: Article 39 of the Exit-Entry Administration Law of the People's Republic of China requires foreigners staying at non-hotel accommodation to register with the local public security organ within 24 hours of arrival.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Hotels and licensed serviced apartments report guest data to the PSB automatically — no separate action required by guests staying there. However, foreigners renting from private landlords must register personally. Many foreign workers skip this step when moving from a hotel into a rented apartment and only discover the obligation during Residence Permit renewal. Non-compliance is an offence under Article 90 (fine up to CNY 2,000). Re-registration is required within 24 hours whenever the residential address changes.
non_obvious_action_required: Go to the local 派出所 (police substation — not the main PSB office) with: passport, lease agreement, and landlord identity card. Landlord presence speeds the process. Some cities (e.g. Shanghai) offer online registration through the local PSB app. Re-register within 24 hours whenever changing address. Keep the registration certificate as it is required for Residence Permit applications.
source: Exit-Entry Administration Law of the People's Republic of China (2012) — Article 39

step: Employer converts Work Permit Notification to issued Foreigner's Work Permit card at local MOHRSS bureau
authority: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) — local Human Resources and Social Security Bureau
form_name: 外国人工作许可证 (Foreigner's Work Permit)
deadline_label: Within 15 days of employee commencing work; card is a prerequisite for the Residence Permit application
source: MOHRSS — Regulations on Work Permits for Foreigners Working in China

step: Obtain Certificate of Coverage from home-country authority to claim totalization agreement exemption before social insurance registration
authority: Home-country social security authority; Chinese local Social Insurance Administration
form_name: Certificate of Coverage (country-specific form name varies by bilateral treaty)
field_label: Social Insurance Totalization Certificate of Coverage
deadline_label: Before social insurance registration; retroactive exemption claims are complex and not guaranteed
non_obvious_official_guidance: China's bilateral totalization agreements allow eligible foreign employees to be exempt from contributing to specified Chinese social insurance schemes if they continue contributing to their home-country social security system.
non_obvious_actual_reality: China has concluded totalization agreements with Germany, South Korea, Denmark, Finland, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Spain, Japan, France, Luxembourg, Serbia, Canada, and others. Scope differs by treaty: most cover pension and unemployment; medical, work injury, and maternity insurance are generally still mandatory in China regardless. The Certificate of Coverage must be obtained from the home-country authority BEFORE local registration — once contributions are withheld, retroactive claims require a formal written application and are not always accepted.
non_obvious_action_required: Before departure, verify whether the employee's home country has a totalization agreement with China. If yes, request a Certificate of Coverage from the relevant home-country authority (e.g. URSSAF for France, DRV for Germany). Present the certificate to the local Chinese Social Insurance Bureau at the time of registration to claim exemption. Retain copies for the employee's file.

step: Employer registers foreign employee for mandatory social insurance at local Social Insurance Administration
authority: Local Social Insurance Administration (社会保险局) under MOHRSS
form_name: 社会保险参保登记表 (Social Insurance Enrollment Registration Form)
deadline_label: Within 30 days of employment commencement; concurrent with Residence Permit application
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the Interim Measures for Foreigners Working in China to Participate in Social Insurance (effective October 2011), foreign employees holding a Foreigner's Work Permit are required to participate in five social insurance schemes: pension, medical, unemployment, work injury, and maternity insurance.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Total employer-plus-employee contribution rates are substantial: employer approximately 28–31%, employee approximately 10–11% of the capped contribution base (rates vary by city and are updated annually). Housing Provident Fund (公积金) is technically mandatory by law for all employees, but enforcement for foreign nationals is inconsistent across cities — some cities permit foreigners to opt out; others require participation. Without a valid totalization Certificate of Coverage, full five-scheme contributions are mandatory from day one.
non_obvious_action_required: Register through the local Social Insurance Administration (integrated with the tax bureau platform in most cities since 2019). Present: Residence Permit, Work Permit card, employment contract, company registration documents, and totalization Certificate of Coverage if applicable. Ensure payroll is configured to calculate and remit contributions monthly before the first salary run.
source: Interim Measures for Foreigners Working in China to Participate in Social Insurance (2011)

step: Employer registers as IIT withholding agent and configures monthly Individual Income Tax withholding
authority: State Taxation Administration (STA) — local tax bureau (税务局)
form_name: 扣缴义务人登记表 (Withholding Agent Registration Form)
deadline_label: Before first salary payment; IIT must be withheld and remitted by the 15th of the following month
source: State Taxation Administration — Individual Income Tax Law of the PRC (amended 2018)

step: Apply for Work-type Residence Permit at local Exit-Entry Administration Bureau within 30 days of Z visa entry
authority: National Immigration Administration (NIA) — local Exit-Entry Administration Bureau (出入境管理局)
form_name: 居留许可申请表 (Residence Permit Application Form)
field_label: Work-type Residence Permit (工作类居留许可)
deadline_label: Within 30 days of entry on Z visa; overstay attracts fines of CNY 500 per day up to a maximum of CNY 10,000
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreigners who enter China on a Z visa must apply for a Residence Permit within 30 days of entry. The Residence Permit is the primary long-term stay authorisation and replaces the Z visa stamp as the lawful residence document.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Residence Permit is a separate document from the Work Permit — both must be valid simultaneously. The initial permit is typically valid for 1 year; multi-year permits (up to 5 years) may be issued for senior employees or on renewal. Biometric data (fingerprints, photo) are collected at the EAB. Most major cities now require advance online appointment booking — walk-in applications may be refused. The Foreigner's Work Permit card must already be in hand at the time of this application, making the sequencing of steps 6 and 10 critical.
non_obvious_action_required: Book an online appointment through the local EAB or NIA app as early as possible after arrival. Gather: passport with Z visa entry stamp, Foreigner's Work Permit card, 2 passport-size photos, completed application form, employment contract, company business licence, physical examination certificate, and PSB temporary residence registration certificate (if staying in private accommodation). Allow 5–15 business days for issuance.
source: National Immigration Administration — Work-type Residence Permit

step: Monitor Individual Income Tax residency status under the 183-day annual physical presence rule
deadline_label: Track from 1 January each calendar year; status determines whether worldwide or China-source-only income is taxable in China
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under Article 1 of the Individual Income Tax Law (amended 2018), a resident individual is one with a domicile in China, or with no domicile but residing in China for 183 or more days in a tax year. Resident individuals are subject to IIT on worldwide income; non-residents on China-source income only.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 183-day count runs on the Gregorian calendar year (1 January to 31 December), not a rolling 12-month window. Both full days and partial days of physical presence in China count. International business trips, personal vacations, and transit through China with an overnight stay all count as presence days. A mid-year shift from non-resident to resident status creates a retroactive worldwide-income exposure from 1 January of that year unless a tax treaty tiebreaker article applies.
non_obvious_action_required: Maintain a detailed personal travel diary from day one of assignment, logging every entry and exit with dates and purpose. Brief the employee before assignment on the financial impact of crossing the 183-day threshold. Consult a tax adviser before any year-end international travel that might affect residency status. Keep passport entry and exit stamps as supporting evidence.
source: Individual Income Tax Law of the People's Republic of China (amended 2018) — Article 1

step: Track the six-consecutive-year rule for foreign-source income exemption from IIT
deadline_label: Applies from Year 1 of Chinese tax residency; a single overseas absence of 30 or more consecutive days in any calendar year resets the counter to zero
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the Individual Income Tax Law Implementation Regulations (2018), a non-domiciled resident individual who has resided in China for fewer than six consecutive years is exempt from IIT on foreign-source income paid and borne entirely by a foreign entity outside China.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The six-year counter accumulates only calendar years in which the individual qualifies as a Chinese tax resident (183+ days present). A single trip of 30 or more consecutive days outside China in any calendar year resets the counter to zero for that year. This creates a planning incentive: employees approaching year six — when they would become fully worldwide-taxable — sometimes deliberately arrange a qualifying 30-day overseas trip to reset the clock and preserve the exemption for a further cycle. Tax authorities are aware of this practice and may scrutinise travel with no apparent business purpose.
non_obvious_action_required: Track the consecutive-year count from the first year of residency. In year 4 or 5, model the tax cost of reaching year 6 versus resetting. If resetting is the chosen strategy, plan the 30+ consecutive day absence carefully and document it fully (passport stamps, hotel receipts, boarding passes). Consult a tax adviser — deliberate resets without business purpose may attract scrutiny.
source: Individual Income Tax Law Implementation Regulations 2018 (国务院令第707号)

step: Assess and monitor permanent establishment (PE) risk created by the employee's activities in China
field_label: PE Risk — Enterprise Income Tax Exposure
deadline_label: Review at assignment commencement and at least annually; PE crystallises on facts, not formal application
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under China's Enterprise Income Tax Law and the OECD-aligned provisions in China's tax treaties, a foreign enterprise may be deemed to have a PE in China if an employee has authority to habitually conclude contracts on behalf of the enterprise, or if a fixed place of business is maintained in China for a period specified in the applicable treaty (typically 6 or 12 months).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Chinese tax authorities have become significantly more assertive in PE assessments since 2018. A single employee with a home office in China, habitually signing contracts or NDAs, or acting as the primary point of contact for Chinese clients, can trigger PE attribution. Consequences include Enterprise Income Tax at 25% on profits attributable to the PE plus interest and penalties. Risk is frequently underestimated for assignments described internally as 'short-term' or 'temporary'.
non_obvious_action_required: Before assignment commencement, review the applicable tax treaty between China and the employer's home country to identify the PE threshold. Define and document the employee's job scope to avoid grant of contract-conclusion authority. Implement a PE monitoring protocol including periodic review of the employee's actual activities. Obtain a combined PE and IIT analysis from qualified tax counsel in both jurisdictions before the assignment starts.
source: Enterprise Income Tax Law of the People's Republic of China — State Taxation Administration

step: File annual Individual Income Tax reconciliation return (汇算清缴) with the tax bureau
authority: State Taxation Administration (STA) — local tax bureau
form_name: 个人所得税年度汇算清缴申报表 (Annual IIT Reconciliation Return)
deadline_label: 1 March to 30 June of the calendar year following the tax year; obligation exists from tax year 2019 onward
responsible_party: Foreign worker (self-file via STA personal tax app or in person at local tax bureau)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Resident individuals are required to file an annual IIT reconciliation return if their annual income exceeds CNY 120,000, their withheld tax differs from the annual liability, or they have income from two or more sources.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The annual reconciliation requirement was introduced in 2019 and is new enough that many employees (and some employers) are unaware of it. Employees with income only from a single Chinese employer, no overseas income, and tax fully withheld correctly may owe nothing further and face minimal risk from non-filing. However, those with overseas income, equity compensation (RSUs, stock options, phantom shares), split payroll, or multiple income sources in China will typically need to file and may face additional liability. Foreign nationals must register on the 个人所得税 app using a Chinese mobile phone number — those without one may need to file in person at the local tax bureau.
non_obvious_action_required: Register on the STA's personal tax app before March 1. Gather all prior-year income documentation including overseas income if applicable. If the employee received equity compensation, obtain vesting or exercise records and consult a tax adviser on the taxable event timing and amount. File (or confirm nil-filing obligation) before 30 June to avoid late-filing penalties.
source: State Taxation Administration — Annual IIT Reconciliation (汇算清缴)

step: Employer remits monthly social insurance and Housing Provident Fund contributions to the tax bureau by the 15th of the following month
authority: Local tax bureau (社会保险费征收) and local Housing Provident Fund Management Centre
field_label: Monthly Social Insurance and Housing Provident Fund Contributions
deadline_label: Monthly; due by the 15th of the following month; late payment attracts a daily penalty of 0.05% of overdue amount
responsible_party: Employer (deducts employee portion from salary; remits combined amount)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers must remit five social insurance contributions (pension, medical, unemployment, work injury, maternity) monthly. Since 2019, social insurance contributions in most provinces are collected by the tax bureau (国家税务局), not the Social Insurance Administration directly.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Housing Provident Fund (公积金) is technically mandatory for all employees under Chinese law, including foreigners. However, enforcement is inconsistent: some cities explicitly permit foreign nationals to opt out; others require full participation. HPF contributions (typically 5–12% employer plus 5–12% employee of capped salary) can only be withdrawn for housing purchases or rental in China, making them of limited utility for employees who will ultimately leave. Contribution bases and rates are updated annually (usually July) and vary by city.
non_obvious_action_required: Configure payroll to remit via the local tax bureau's electronic payment system. Verify the current contribution rates and base caps annually. Confirm the Housing Provident Fund status for foreign nationals with the local HPF bureau before the first contribution cycle. Keep all contribution receipts — these are needed for social insurance certificates upon the employee's departure.
source: Social Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (2010) — Article 60

step: Employer initiates Foreigner's Work Permit renewal via MOHRSS platform at least 30 days before permit expiry
authority: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) — local bureau
form_name: 外国人工作许可证续签申请 (Work Permit Renewal Application)
deadline_label: Apply minimum 30 days before permit expiry; working on an expired permit is a criminal offence under Article 80 of the Exit-Entry Administration Law
non_obvious_official_guidance: The Foreigner's Work Permit must be renewed before its expiry date. Renewal is applied for by the employer through the MOHRSS online platform.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Work Permit is strictly tied to the specific employer, city, and registered job position. A change of employer requires a new Work Permit Notification and typically exit and re-entry on a new Z visa — there is no in-country transfer mechanism. A significant role change within the same employer (different position category) may require an amendment application. If the permit lapses, the employee must stop work immediately; employing a foreigner without a valid work permit exposes the employer to fines and potential business licence consequences.
non_obvious_action_required: Diarise work permit and Residence Permit expiry dates together — both must remain valid simultaneously. Begin renewal at least 30 days before expiry. If an employer change is planned, engage an immigration adviser well in advance to avoid gaps in work authorisation. Inform the employee not to travel internationally during the renewal window if holding a single-entry Residence Permit.
source: MOHRSS — Regulations on Work Permits for Foreigners Working in China

step: Renew Work-type Residence Permit at local Exit-Entry Administration Bureau before expiry
authority: National Immigration Administration (NIA) — local Exit-Entry Administration Bureau
form_name: 居留许可续签申请表 (Residence Permit Renewal Application Form)
deadline_label: Apply before expiry; overstay accrues fines from day 1; no automatic grace period
source: National Immigration Administration — Residence Permit Management

step: Claim pension insurance personal-account lump-sum refund upon permanent departure from China
form_name: 社会保险待遇领取申请表 (Social Insurance Benefit Claim Form)
field_label: Pension Personal Account Lump-Sum Refund on Departure
deadline_label: After permanent departure; claim before cancelling Residence Permit where possible; time limit set by local bureau
non_obvious_official_guidance: Article 97 of the Social Insurance Law provides that foreigners who leave China permanently may apply for a one-time payment of the balance of their individual pension insurance personal account.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Only the employee's personal contribution account (approximately 8% of salary) is refundable. The employer-contributed pooled portion (approximately 20% of salary) is absorbed into the pooled fund and is non-refundable under any circumstances. Some cities require the employee to be physically present to make the claim; others accept a notarised power of attorney. For employees from totalization-agreement countries, pension portability under the treaty may be more advantageous than a lump-sum refund — model both scenarios before deciding.
non_obvious_action_required: Before the final exit from China, contact the local Social Insurance Administration to confirm the exact claim procedure and required documents. Gather: social insurance contribution statements, work permit, residence permit, Chinese bank account details, and employment termination letter. If using a power of attorney (departing before the refund is processed), have it notarised in China before leaving. Obtain a Social Insurance Certificate (参保证明) as a record for home-country social security purposes.
source: Social Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (2010) — Article 97
